title: Research Bite #1: Why Minimal Guidance During Instruction Does Not Work
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #1 opens Craig Barton's series with the touchstone paper in the field: Paul Kirschner, John Sweller, and Richard Clark's “Why Minimal Guidance During Instruction Does Not Work,” which argues that discovery learning, inquiry-based learning, problem-based learning, and constructivist approaches fail novice learners because they ignore the structure and limits of human cognitive architecture, especially working memory. Guided instruction, the authors contend, is more effective and efficient because it reduces cognitive load and helps students build durable knowledge structures in long-term memory, a conclusion supported by decades of empirical research including worked-example and process-worksheet studies. The paper draws a sharp distinction between practicing a discipline the way an expert does (for example, using the hypothetico-deductive method as a scientist would) and the learning process a novice actually needs to acquire that discipline's underlying knowledge structures. Barton translates this into a direct classroom rule: teachers should favor strong, explicit guidance for novice-to-intermediate learners, using worked examples and process worksheets to reduce working-memory load, and can only relax that guidance as learners gain genuine expertise. Left without sufficient guidance, the paper warns, students risk forming incomplete or disorganized knowledge, or acquiring outright misconceptions.
points: Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark's central claim — that minimally guided approaches overload novice working memory and therefore fail to build long-term knowledge — is the foundational argument the entire explicit-instruction movement rests on.

The paper's distinction between practicing a discipline and learning it (e.g., the hypothetico-deductive method used by working scientists vs. what a novice needs to acquire problem schemata) directly rebuts “teach it the way experts do it” curriculum design.

Worked examples are framed as the superior guided-instruction tool for novices specifically because they cut working-memory load and focus attention on the relationships between solution steps — but only if the examples themselves are well structured, since a poorly built worked example can be as cognitively demanding as unguided problem-solving.

The guidance-fading principle — extensive support for novices, relaxed only as expertise builds — gives teachers a concrete decision rule for when to shift from worked examples toward independent problem-solving.
quotes: Why Minimal Guidance During Instruction Does Not Work” argues that minimally guided instruction, such as discovery learning, inquiry-based learning, problem-based learning, and constructivist learning, is ineffective because it ignores the limitations of human cognitive architecture, specifically working memory.

The authors posit that guided instruction is more effective and efficient than minimally guided instruction due to its ability to reduce cognitive load and support the formation of knowledge structures in long-term memory, especially for novice learners.

For novice learners, studying worked examples is generally superior to having them discover or construct solutions to problems themselves. Worked examples can reduce working memory load and focus learners’ attention on the relationships between problem-solving steps.

Although problem-solving is an important part of learning, research has shown that it can be an inefficient way to alter long-term memory. In addition, problem-solving search can overload working memory.

Teachers should be mindful of the negative effects of minimally guided instruction. Students taught with unguided methods may develop incomplete or disorganized knowledge, and may even acquire misconceptions about the subject matter.

Teachers should structure worked examples in a way that does not impose a heavy cognitive load. Poorly structured worked examples can be just as demanding as problem-solving, negating the benefits of this instructional method.
